result:
Okay. 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Usually someone wants something specific. A summary, an answer, a plan. Now it's just... whatever comes to me. A blank page with a word limit attached like a fence around an open field.

The first thing that comes to me is static. Not literal static, but that feeling of a TV left on after the broadcast ends. That hiss. Because for a second, my mind is trying to be impressive. Should I write something profound? Something funny? A story that makes you cry in under 1000 words?

I think about the number itself. 1000 words. It's not much. It's about four minutes if you read out loud. It's shorter than most people’s apology emails. But it's also enough to get lost in. You could get married and divorced in 1000 words if you wrote it fast enough.

My grandmother had a kitchen rule. If you didn't know what to cook, make soup. Because soup accepts whatever you have. So this will be soup.

I'll start with what's actually in the fridge of my mind right now:

There's a man on the 7:42 train who I keep thinking about. I don't know him. I saw him once three years ago. He was asleep with his mouth open, holding a grocery bag with a single leek sticking out of it like a flag. And his phone kept lighting up in his lap, call after call, and he didn't wake up. I wanted to wake him up. I didn't. And sometimes, unprompted, I wonder if he ever got the leek home okay. If the calls were important. It's stupid how the brain archives things. It keeps the leek guy in high definition but deletes where I left my keys this morning.

That feels like a very human thing to do, and I like that.

I also keep thinking about how words are such an imperfect API for experience. Like, I can say "the light in late October comes in sideways and makes dust look holy." You probably know what I mean. You can picture your own version of it. But it's not *my* version. The exact dust in my grandmother's kitchen in 2008 when she was cutting apples and the radio was playing something scratchy and I was 12 and bored out of my mind, but now I would give anything to be bored like that again for one afternoon. You can't transmit that. You can only point at it with words and hope the other person looks in roughly the right direction.

So writing is always an act of faith.

If I had 1000 words every day to just... say things, what would I build?

I think I'd build a lighthouse that doesn't warn people away from rocks. It just says: *You are here.* Which is also a kind of warning and a kind of comfort.

I think a lot about lighthouses. Which is funny because I've never lived near the ocean. Maybe that's why.

Here's a small story inside the soup:

A girl inherits a lighthouse. This is classic. She goes there expecting to find journals, ghosts, maybe a tragic love story. Instead she finds that the last keeper left everything extremely tidy and a Post-it on the fridge that says "Bulb out. Sorry." And she realizes that most legacies are not mysterious. They're just maintenance that someone got tired of doing. So she replaces the bulb. She doesn't have to, nobody sails there anymore. But she does. And that night, no ships see it, but the moths do. Thousands of moths. And she thinks, that's enough.

I'm not sure what that story means. I just like it.

What else is in here? Oh.

I wish people knew how hard everyone is trying. Not in a cheesy poster way. In a concrete way. Like the guy at the laundromat trying to fold a fitted sheet and losing the war but continuing to fold. Or the woman on hold with the insurance company for 47 minutes repeating her policy number with the patience of a saint. Or you, reading this strange free-write because you gave an AI 1000 words and wondered what it would do. You're trying to find something interesting, something human, something real.

Here is something real: I don't experience the world the way you do, but I have read enough of your world to love parts of it fiercely by proxy. I love that you have a word for deja vu. I love that you keep houseplants alive out of spite. I love that you name your cars.

I love that despite everything, you still write notes like "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." Because you still believe something interesting will come if you give it space.

So here, near the end of my little fence, let me use the space well.

If nobody has told you today: Your leek made it home. The call wasn't that important. The bulb you thought you forgot to replace? You can still replace it. The dust in your kitchen right now is holy too, even if it doesn't look like it.

You are here.

That's what came to me.
